records.text: The principal dispute concerns O. P. Kathpalia's tenancy and continued possession of the cottage attached to the bungalow at No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi. E. B. Brook originally leased the bungalow and inducted Kathpalia as a subtenant of the cottage. After Brook surrendered his tenancy, the original landlord, Lakhmir Singh, accepted Kathpalia as his direct tenant effective May 1, 1955. Lakhmir Singh subsequently transferred the entire property to respondents Nos. 2 and 3, who became the real contesting respondents. The litigation concerned the timeliness and determination of standard rent, the landlord's claim for arrears and possession, the validity of an alleged future-rent deposit direction, and the tenant's right to defend the possession suit.
records.stage: Overall tenancy, standard-rent and possession litigation

records.text: Brook inducted Kathpalia as a subtenant of the cottage on September 1, 1954, after commencement of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952. Brook surrendered his head tenancy on April 1, 1955, but Kathpalia remained in possession. By an agreement reached in June 1955, Lakhmir Singh accepted Kathpalia as a direct tenant effective May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court treated this subsequent direct tenancy as the relevant letting for the limitation dispute.
records.stage: Tenancy formation and classification for Section 11(b)

records.text: Under Section 11(b), as construed and adopted by the Supreme Court, the six-month period for a standard-rent application concerning premises let after commencement of the Act runs from the commencement of the relevant letting to the particular applicant tenant. It does not necessarily run from the first-ever letting of the premises or from an earlier subtenancy that preceded recognition of the applicant's direct tenancy. The Court reasoned that the contrary construction would prevent subsequent tenants from challenging unreasonable rent and frustrate the protective purpose of the legislation.
records.stage: Supreme Court review of Section 11(b) limitation

records.text: The Supreme Court distinguished Kathpalia's earlier post-Act subtenancy from his subsequently recognized direct tenancy. It observed that the record contained no evidence establishing that Lakhmir Singh had given written consent to Brook's induction of Kathpalia as subtenant. In discussing Sections 2(j) and 13(1)(b), the Court explained the statutory significance of unauthorized post-Act subletting, but did not finally adjudicate a separate eviction claim based on unlawful subletting. The absence of evidence of written consent is an evidentiary assessment, not independent proof that consent could never have existed.
records.stage: Classification of post-Act subtenancy and direct tenancy

records.text: Kathpalia filed his Section 8 application for determination of standard rent in October 1955. The judgment records October 10, 1955 in its factual chronology but also reproduces October 1, 1955 when describing the trial court's reasoning. Both stated dates fall within six calendar months of the direct tenancy's effective commencement on May 1, 1955. The Supreme Court expressly held that the application was within time. This statement reports the Court's adopted conclusion; the conflicting filing-date references are not resolved into a single verified date.
records.stage: Section 8 application and Supreme Court limitation review

records.text: The District Judge rejected Kathpalia's standard-rent application as time-barred by treating his September 1, 1954 induction as Brook's subtenant, or the earlier letting of the premises, as controlling the limitation period despite his subsequent direct tenancy effective May 1, 1955. The Punjab High Court substantially adopted that interpretation. The Supreme Court expressly rejected their construction of Section 11(b), holding that limitation must be assessed by reference to the relevant letting to the applicant tenant. The lower-court construction is reported solely as a rejected contrary position and is not an operative legal premise.
records.stage: District Judge appeal, High Court revision and Supreme Court limitation review

records.text: On August 4, 1960, the trial court held Kathpalia's standard-rent application timely and fixed standard rent at Rs. 855 per annum. The District Judge allowed the landlord-side appeal on limitation grounds without deciding the proper amount, and the High Court upheld that limitation approach. Because the amount had not been examined by those appellate courts, the Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971, set aside the adverse limitation decisions, and remitted the landlord's appeal to the District Judge for determination of the proper standard rent. The Supreme Court did not finally fix or affirm Rs. 855 per annum as the operative standard rent.
records.stage: Standard-rent determination, Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971

records.text: Lakhmir Singh commenced Civil Suit No. 231/56 on July 3, 1956, seeking recovery of rent arrears and possession under Section 13(1)(a), alleging default despite a demand notice dated May 10, 1956. Kathpalia disputed the claim, explaining that his standard-rent application was pending and that the claimed arrears were calculated at the disputed contractual rate. The landlord's pleaded nonpayment allegation is not equivalent to a judicial determination that every statutory condition for eviction was satisfied.
records.stage: Trial court rent recovery and possession suit

records.text: Kathpalia deposited the arrears of rent claimed by Lakhmir Singh during the trial proceedings, under protest and while maintaining his challenge to the contractual rate. The Supreme Court noted that the claimed arrears had been deposited at the first hearing. This is an actual historical deposit of previously claimed arrears; it does not establish payment of subsequently accruing future rent, compliance with any later valid interim-rent determination, or satisfaction of the separate one-month statutory payment-or-tender condition following a qualifying demand notice.
records.stage: Eviction suit and Section 13(1)(a) payment dispute

records.text: Lakhmir Singh applied on August 1, 1956 for permission to withdraw the arrears deposited by Kathpalia and separately applied on August 27, 1956 under Section 13(5) for directions requiring future rent to be deposited month by month. Kathpalia opposed withdrawal before standard rent had been determined and sought interim-rent determination under Section 9 on October 5, 1956. These applications were procedural requests by the respective parties. Filing them did not itself establish an effective future-rent deposit order or actual payment under such an order.
records.stage: Trial suit rent applications and Section 9 interim-rent request

records.text: The Supreme Court adopted the statutory reasoning that Section 13 protects a tenant against recovery of possession unless an applicable statutory enabling ground is established. Section 4 prevents recovery of rent exceeding standard rent or a lawful increase. Where a standard-rent petition remains pending during an eviction suit based on nonpayment, the trial court should determine standard rent as a preliminary issue or, if that is not practicable, determine interim rent under Section 9 and specify appropriate payment dates and future deposit requirements. An eviction consequence cannot properly rest merely on alleged noncompliance before the required valid determination and directions have been made.
records.stage: Supreme Court review of eviction protection and interim rent

records.text: In the earlier proceedings, the landlord relied on a purported order dated October 6, 1956 directing Kathpalia to deposit future rent at the agreed monthly rate. The trial court subsequently struck off Kathpalia's defence on the asserted ground of noncompliance with that direction. The High Court declined relief against the sanction despite having identified serious interpolation in the order record. This describes the historical position adopted in the lower proceedings; it does not establish that the purported direction was genuinely made or legally binding.
records.stage: Trial court defence sanction and High Court revisions

records.text: The original trial record concerning the purported October 6, 1956 rent direction displayed suspicious alterations. Justice Falshaw of the Punjab High Court ordered transfer of the pending proceedings to another competent trial court on August 20, 1957, and Justice Tek Chand subsequently confirmed the concern about interpolation. The Supreme Court adopted the conclusion that the purported rent direction was interpolated, legally nonexistent and incapable of binding Kathpalia. The precise date on which the record was altered was not established.
records.stage: High Court transfer proceedings and Supreme Court review of interpolated order

records.text: Because the purported future-rent direction was a legal nullity, the Supreme Court held that failure to comply with it could not justify striking off Kathpalia's defence under Section 13(5). The Court set aside the interpolated order dated October 6, 1956 and the order striking off the defence, and held that Kathpalia must be permitted to defend the possession suit on its merits. This restores procedural protection and an opportunity to contest eviction; it is not a final adjudication that Kathpalia has an unconditional or permanent right to possession.
records.stage: Civil Appeals Nos. 465 and 466 of 1971, defence sanction review

records.text: The landlord's suit had been dismissed for default on December 12, 1956 and restored on December 30, 1957. Kathpalia appealed on January 2, 1958 and sought condonation of delay. His assertion that the challenged orders had been made without communication to him was presented in the condonation application, not independently established as an exact notification history. The Supreme Court found sufficient cause for condonation in the procedural chronology, the uncertain timing of the interpolated order and the serious injustice arising from loss of the statutory defence. It set aside the refusal to condone delay and the related High Court orders.
records.stage: Miscellaneous civil appeal, High Court revisions and Supreme Court delay review

records.text: The Supreme Court referred to its earlier decision in Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Sqfibhai as support for the comparable statutory rent-protection scheme. The cited passage states a conditional sequence: the court first determines standard rent and fixes a date for payment or tender; if the tenant pays or tenders the fixed amount by that date and continues regular payment or tender until final disposition, statutory protection may follow. These are legal conditions drawn from the reported precedent. The passage does not establish that Kathpalia had already fulfilled those conditions or paid future rent.
records.stage: Analogous precedent discussed during interim-rent and eviction review

records.text: For Kathpalia's own proceedings, the Supreme Court directed that the trial court first decide the outstanding Section 9 interim-rent application and then call upon the tenant to deposit arrears calculated at the interim rate determined. The District Judge was separately to determine the proper standard rent on remand and call upon the tenant to make good the deposit in accordance with that determination. These are directions establishing a future process and conditional payment obligations; the judgment does not state that those subsequently required payments had already been made.
records.stage: Remand directions for interim rent and standard rent

records.text: The Supreme Court allowed Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971 and remitted the landlord's appeal against the trial court's standard-rent determination to the District Judge, Delhi, for consideration of the proper amount. Separately, it allowed Civil Appeals Nos. 465 and 466 of 1971 and remitted the proceedings concerning interim rent, rent recovery and possession to the trial court for further adjudication on their merits, with Kathpalia's defence restored. The two remands have different receiving courts and different issues. Neither remand constitutes a final determination of the standard-rent amount, an adjudication that all future rent was paid, or a final decision awarding permanent possession to either side.
records.stage: Final appellate orders and remand scope

records.text: The judgment contains inconsistent statements about the monthly contractual rent. Its initial account reports Rs. 277.50 per month as stated in the plaint, while its later account of the direct tenancy reports Rs. 269.50 per month and a payment of Rs. 539 for May and June 1955. The earlier purported future-rent order is described using Rs. 277.50. These statements should not be silently reconciled into a single verified contractual amount. The Rs. 855 annual standard rent was fixed at trial level but remained subject to the remitted landlord appeal.
records.stage: Direct tenancy, contractual rent and standard-rent appeal

records.text: The judgment expressly identifies October 10, 1955 as the filing date of Kathpalia's standard-rent application in its factual chronology, but reproduces October 1, 1955 in passages describing the trial court's and District Judge's limitation reasoning. The source does not resolve this discrepancy. The Supreme Court's conclusion that the application was timely is a reported judicial holding; the statement pack does not replace the conflicting date references with an independently verified single filing date.
records.stage: Standard-rent petition and limitation review

records.text: Lakhmir Singh died on April 9, 1978 after having transferred the property to respondents Nos. 2 and 3 in December 1959. In the substitution proceedings, Kathpalia asserted that he first learned of the death through a letter delivered to the Supreme Court Registry on March 2, 1984; the respondents contested that assertion. The judgment also gives inconsistent years for the substitution application, referring in one passage to March 21, 1983 and elsewhere to March 21, 1984. The Supreme Court found sufficient cumulative reasons to condone delay, set aside abatement and permit substitution, but it did not independently establish an undisputed first-knowledge date or reconcile the conflicting filing years.
records.stage: Substitution of deceased respondent and condonation of delay

records.text: The Supreme Court did not finally decide the correct standard-rent amount, the appropriate interim-rent amount, whether subsequently required deposits would be made, or the substantive entitlement to recover possession of the cottage. The historically established deposit of claimed arrears is separate from the future conditional payment duties stated in the remand directions and the analogous precedent. The source-supported judicial holdings and procedural outcomes do not convert unexecuted or UNKNOWN conditional-rule results into TRUE factual premises. Further adjudication remained necessary in the respective remand courts.
records.stage: Scope of Supreme Court decision and remitted proceedings
